executive_summary: CAD/CHF closed at 0.59021 on 30 October 2026. That is the number of Swiss francs one Canadian dollar buys, so a rising pair means a stronger Canadian dollar. The pair is up 1.00% over one month, 2.60% over three months and 3.31% over six months. It sits at the 94th percentile of its 52-week closing range, 18 pips below the 52-week closing high of 0.59203 set on 28 October. Over the past six months it has traded as a franc-funded carry trade. The Bank of Canada now holds a 250bp policy advantage over the SNB's 0%, and a rolled futures position earns about 283bp a year. Spot has drifted higher even though Canada's fundamentals have weakened. Looking at the two currencies together shows more than either currency's view against the US dollar, which is close to neutral for both. Three things stand out. Growth: Canada is growing 0.95% a year against Switzerland's 2.63%. Policy path: the market prices the 250bp policy gap to keep widening, while both central banks are more likely to narrow it. Oil and haven demand: in this cross they partly cancel, which leaves Canada's growth shortfall exposed. This analysis is Bearish tactically (score -0.1291, conviction 2) and Bearish strategically (score -0.2682, conviction 2). The targets are 0.5850 by end-November and 0.5750 by end-April 2027. There are two caveats. First, carry means the six-month forward already sits at about 0.5819, so the strategic edge over forwards is only about 68 pips. Second, the daily chart runs against the call: spot is above a bullishly stacked 50/100/200-day average set with higher highs. The trade is therefore one to build on rallies, not to chase.

market_context.valuation_assessment: On long-run measures the Canadian dollar is cheap against the franc. PPP (World Bank 2025 conversion factors, flagged as best available) puts fair value at about 0.7978, so CAD is roughly 26% undervalued; seen from the franc side, CHF is 35.2% expensive against CAD. BIS real effective exchange rates for September 2026 are Canada 95.59 and Switzerland 98.37, both at the 3rd percentile of their 33 monthly readings since January 2024, so neither currency is rich on recent real history. Spot at 0.59021 prices a persistent tariff discount on Canada and a structural haven premium on the franc. Neither PPP gap has closed on a 1-6 month horizon before. Valuation therefore informs the upside tail (a tariff deal), not the central path. The 52-week intraday range is 0.56016 to 0.59295 (92nd percentile); spot is 271 pips (+4.81%) above the 52-week closing low.

market_context.recent_regime: Through September the pair ground higher from August as carry was rebuilt. On 1-2 October a sharp franc rally knocked it from 0.58726 (30 September close) to an intraday low of 0.57893. In mid-October it held a 0.5810-0.5880 band while French sovereign stress drove haven buying of francs, mostly against the euro. On 22-28 October it rallied 63 pips (0.58573 to 0.59203) as WTI ran to USD 102 and the Bank of Canada hiked. On 30 October a wide 44-pip intraday range (0.58696-0.59136) ended near its high at 0.59021. In short, the regime is oil plus carry lifting the pair, against haven demand that has been aimed at the euro rather than the Canadian dollar.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: Policy differential: Bank of Canada 2.50% (hiked 28 October) vs SNB 0.00% = +250bp for a long CAD/CHF position. The daily central-bank policy series still read 2.25% on 26 October because it lags announcements, so its 225bp gap is out of date. The futures roll, the annualised premium between the December and March CME contracts observed 29 October, is -283.1bp: CAD/CHF trades at a forward discount, so a long position earns that much as it rolls (combining the expected rate path with any cross-currency basis). Two-year yields are Canada 3.31% vs Switzerland 0.18% = 313bp, so the curve prices further widening. Carry-to-vol is 250bp / 5.093% three-month implied estimate = 0.49 (0.48 on 60-day realised vol of 5.21%; about 0.54-0.56 on the 283bp futures premium). The true ratio is probably somewhat lower because the implied estimate runs low, but it is still the best carry-to-vol of any CAD cross. Carry is working: the pair is up 3.31% over six months before carry, so a long position has earned about 4.7% including it. Short CAD/CHF is the most expensive CAD short in the G10. On the pure 250bp policy gap the six-month points would be -73.8 pips (0.58283); the extra roughly 10 pips reflects the second Bank of Canada hike priced for early 2027, plus any basis. Carry is a cost for any bearish expression, not evidence on direction.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The policy gap is 250bp in the Canadian dollar's favour. The Bank of Canada raised its overnight target to 2.50% on 28 October, and the SNB rate is 0%. The BIS-compiled daily policy-rate series still showed 2.25% for Canada on 26 October because it lags announcements, so the 225bp gap it implies is out of date. Further along the curve the gap is wider: 313bp at two years (Government of Canada 3.31% against the Swiss 0.18% on 30 October) and about 333bp at ten years on end-October closes (329bp on September monthly averages). So the curve already prices further widening. The annualised gap between December and March Canadian dollar and Swiss franc futures, observed on 29 October, is 283bp. That is about 33bp more than the policy gap, which fits a second Bank of Canada hike being priced for early 2027, plus any cross-currency basis. Neither bank meets within four weeks: the next decisions are 9 December for the Bank of Canada and 10 December for the SNB. Until then the differential can only be repriced through data, and that is scored under Factor 2. Carry earns a long CAD/CHF position about 0.2% over four weeks, but forwards already deduct it. Carry makes the pair expensive to short; it is not evidence that spot should rise. The rate signal is balanced at this horizon.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the question is whether the 250bp gap widens as far as the curve implies. The Canadian two-year sits 81bp above the policy rate. Commerzbank noted on 28 October that markets had priced four Bank of Canada hikes by September 2027, though some of that was trimmed after the weak 30 October GDP release. The Swiss two-year has fallen to 0.18% from 0.263% on 30 September, so it prices almost no SNB tightening. Our Canadian research expects one more hike at most and gives a 40% chance that the Bank stops at 2.50%. CPI-trim (1.8%) and CPI-median (1.9%) are below target, and third-quarter growth is tracking 1.3% against the Bank's 2.0%. Bank of America also argued that weak activity limits sustained tightening. On the Swiss side we see a 30% chance of a first SNB hike by March 2027 as headline inflation rises from 1.0%, against near-zero pricing. Both legs point to a narrower gap than priced. The Swiss date is the bigger test: 9 December is a bare Bank of Canada statement, while the 10 December SNB assessment brings a new conditional inflation forecast. The first Bank of Canada decision of 2027 is not in the published schedule we hold. Carry stays positive for the pair throughout, which holds confidence to 52.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The growth gap runs firmly against Canada. OECD figures put Swiss GDP up 2.63% on the year against 0.95% for Canada, and the gap is widening. Canadian August GDP was flat, September is estimated at -0.1%, and employment fell 68,300 in September with unemployment rising to 6.5%. Swiss momentum is cooling from a high level: the KOF barometer slipped to 107.6 in October from 109.1 and the PMI is 55.3. Swiss registered unemployment is still only 3.1%. On inflation the two economies are converging, which matters for policy. Canadian headline is 3.1%, but CPI-trim and CPI-median are 1.8-1.9% and falling, so the case for more hikes rests on gasoline prices. Swiss headline has risen to 1.0%, its fastest since September 2024, and that rise is what creates an SNB hike option. Canadian data move this pair more, because the market has priced a January hike on the assumption that the labour market stabilises. Swiss data matter mainly through the SNB option. The Canadian calendar is dense over the next four weeks: trade on 4 November, employment on 6 November, CPI on 16 November and third-quarter GDP on 30 November, against Swiss CPI on 3 November. Canada's October releases mostly surprised to the downside, so the surprise gap favours the franc.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months the growth gap should stay in Switzerland's favour. SECO raised its 2026 forecast to 1.7% and holds 1.6% for 2027. The Bank of Canada's 2.0% for 2027 looks optimistic against a Reuters poll median of 1.7% and our 1.5%, and Canadian housing is contracting, with September sales down 7.7% on the year. Inflation paths are converging. Canadian core is below 2% while the headline is propped up by oil. Swiss inflation is drifting up from the lowest level in the G10 toward the SNB's projected 0.7-0.8%, and Brent above the levels assumed in the SNB's September forecast tilts that higher. Convergence matters because it argues for a narrower policy gap: a Bank of Canada that cannot justify the second hike already priced, against an SNB that may move off zero in 2027. The main risk to this view is Canadian business inflation expectations. One-year expectations are 3.7% in the Business Outlook Survey, and sustained oil above USD 100 could lift Canadian core to about 2.3% by early 2027, which would validate more hikes. Swiss growth figures are also noisy because pharmaceutical swings drove most of the second quarter, which limits confidence.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: CAD/CHF has a moderate positive beta to global risk appetite. The beta is lower than AUD/CHF's because the US linkage anchors the Canadian dollar. The backdrop is deteriorating at the margin rather than breaking. The VIX was 17.2 on 29 October, mid-range but up 1.16 points on the month, while US investment-grade spreads (89bp) and high-yield spreads (326bp) are at the 96th and 95th percentiles of their one-year ranges. The franc's haven role has revived around French fiscal and political stress, with the OAT-Bund spread at 152.5bp on 20 October, its widest since 2011. Asset managers have been cutting franc shorts. That flow is euro-specific and reaches CAD/CHF only partly. Equities at records argue against a broad risk-off, which caps confidence: the SMI rose 8.72% in October and the TSX is 17.71% higher on the year. The oil rally is driven by supply, so it is not a risk-appetite signal for this pair and is scored under Factor 5. On balance, wider credit spreads and a live haven bid tilt the factor mildly against the pair.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months the risk regime could resolve either way, and the outcomes push this pair in both directions. A French budget failure or a US equity correction from record levels would favour the franc. A dovish Fed repricing after the midterms, which Brown Brothers Harriman sees as the main risk to the dollar, would support risk-sensitive currencies such as CAD over havens. The Middle East is unusually two-sided for this cross. Escalation lifts oil, which supports CAD, and lifts haven demand, which supports CHF. A settlement removes both. Much of the oil-haven exposure therefore nets out within CAD/CHF. Gold, which tends to move with the franc, fell 7.03% in October, removing a supporting cross-asset signal for CHF. National Bank of Canada also finds the Canadian dollar more correlated with gold than with oil lately, which further dilutes gold's net effect on the pair. With the main tails roughly offsetting, the strategic signal is Neutral at low confidence. It would turn Bearish if the VIX held above 25 or US high-yield spreads rose above 400bp.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months positioning matters less than the flows behind it, and those flows are balanced for this pair. The Canadian dollar leveraged short has been in place every week since May, between -37,663 and -102,495 contracts. It is funded by negative carry against the US dollar, so it can persist without a catalyst. The franc short has built steadily from -4,823 in late May and tracks the widening gap between the SNB and its peers. Both leveraged books are tied to US dollar carry rather than to a view on CAD/CHF, and no real-money group is leaning on the cross. Swiss institutions hold structural hedges on foreign assets, a slow franc-negative that rises with rate gaps. Canadian pension hedge ratios are not disclosed publicly. The one structural event that could force a regime change is a US-Canada tariff deal, which we put at 25-35% over six months. It would squeeze the Canadian dollar short and lift the pair. A euro-area sovereign crisis is the matching franc-positive tail. Positioning is a source of volatility for the pair, not of direction.

If the 6 November employment report stabilises or a tariff deal lands, the larger and more stretched CAD short would cover first and lift CAD/CHF against our view. That is the main contrarian risk.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Terms of trade currently move in Canada's favour. NYMEX WTI rose 14.1% in October to USD 102.00 on supply disruption around Hormuz, a direct terms-of-trade gain for Canada. Switzerland is an energy importer, though energy is only about 3.5% of its CPI basket. Gold, the franc's commodity under our netting rules, fell 7.03% in October, removing a support for CHF. Canada keeps less of the oil rally than headline WTI suggests, because Western Canadian Select traded USD 27 under WTI for November delivery as pipeline egress is full. The realised heavy barrel is still well above year-earlier levels. The September trade release on 4 November should capture the first full month of oil above USD 90. Switzerland's surplus is far larger at 9.2% of GDP, but it is a known structural feature. Its September trade data were distorted by a 130.8% jump in pharmaceutical imports. Bilateral goods trade is small and in Switzerland's favour: Canada exported USD 4.6bn to Switzerland and imported USD 5.8bn in 2024. That is too small to drive the cross. The dynamic part of the external balance favours CAD in the near term.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months the two external positions roughly offset. Switzerland's surplus is large, persistent and diversified. The IMF projects 6.2% of GDP for 2026, the net international investment position is CHF 986bn, and the pharmaceutical tariff regime has settled at 15%. Canada's surplus is smaller and depends on oil, so a settlement with Iran that took USD 15-20 off WTI would erase most of the terms-of-trade gain. Canada also faces a 50% US tariff on C$20bn of exports, Section 232 duties on steel and cars, and a threatened rise to 50% on steel and cars from 1 January 2027. Valuation leans the other way. On flagged World Bank PPP factors the Canadian dollar is roughly 26% undervalued against the franc. Both real effective exchange rates are at the 3rd percentile of their readings since January 2024 (Canada 95.59, Switzerland 98.37), so neither currency is rich on recent real history. That PPP gap has no record of closing within six months, so it informs the tails rather than the central path. On our oil-versus-gold netting, a Middle East settlement would weaken CAD through oil but also remove part of the franc's haven bid, which further limits the net effect. Neutral reflects a durable Swiss surplus against cheaper Canadian valuation and an oil windfall that can disappear.

We see two-sided risks around those assumptions: an Iran settlement on one side, a tariff deal on the other, and the 1 January 2027 deadline in between. So we take no strategic edge here.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: Canada is the world's fourth-largest crude producer, so oil up means CAD strongly up, but realisation is capped by a USD 27 WCS discount and full pipelines. Canada is also a gold producer, and National Bank of Canada finds the currency's recent correlation stronger with gold than with WTI. Natural gas is a mild positive.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: Switzerland imports energy, so oil up is a mild CHF negative; energy is about 3.5% of its CPI basket against roughly 7% in the euro area. Under our rules gold up means CHF up through its safe-haven correlation. Gold refining and transit dominate Swiss goods-flow volatility.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Step 1, oil: rising oil helps CAD strongly and hurts CHF mildly, so the net effect is a rising pair. Step 2, gold: rising gold helps CHF under our rules but also helps CAD through the gold-producer channel National Bank identifies, so the net effect is roughly flat to slightly negative for the pair. Step 3, October: WTI +14.1% and gold -7.03% both favoured the pair, a clean positive for CAD. Step 4, the WCS discount means Canada captures roughly three-quarters of a headline WTI move, which trims the oil effect. Net: the pair is long oil and roughly neutral gold, with oil dominant. The 2024 IMF bilateral data show Swiss-reported imports from Canada of USD 8.5bn against Canadian-reported exports of USD 4.6bn; the gap is likely gold shipments for refining, an inference rather than a measured fact.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: A 10% rise in WTI (to about USD 112) lifts Canadian terms of trade and the current account, a CAD positive of roughly 0.5-0.75% against the US dollar on historical sensitivity. The franc is barely affected unless the rise comes with escalation that adds haven demand. Net, the pair rises, by less than USD/CAD would fall if the move is driven by Hormuz escalation.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: A 10% fall in WTI (to about USD 92) cuts the Canadian windfall, a CAD negative of roughly 0.5-0.75% against the US dollar. If the fall reflects an Iran settlement, the franc also loses part of its haven bid, which cushions the cross. Net, the pair falls, by less than a pure oil move would imply.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: Crude oil, measured at the Canadian realisation of WCS rather than headline WTI. Gold is secondary because it affects both legs in partly offsetting ways.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both central banks turned more hawkish in October, so the near-term signal largely cancels. On 28 October the Bank of Canada hiked and said the Governing Council saw less scope for monetary accommodation and a possible need to raise rates further. Its Monetary Policy Report lifted the end-2026 inflation projection to about 3.4-3.5%. That guidance is conditional, one meeting at a time, and markets have priced roughly what it implies. The SNB's summary of deliberations, published 22 October, said an increased willingness to intervene was no longer necessary. That removes a cap on franc strength while keeping the standard line that the SNB is willing to act in the FX market as necessary. Each change supports its own currency, so in CAD/CHF they largely offset. The next Bank of Canada communication is its summary of deliberations in the week of 9 November. The SNB has nothing scheduled before 10 December. Neither bank's guidance has drifted far from market pricing, so the guidance-pricing gap is near zero on both sides.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months the guidance paths are likely to diverge in the franc's favour. The Bank of Canada's record argues for a short cycle. It held at 2.25% for eleven months before hiking once, and the Reuters poll calls the expected cycle the shortest in 30 years. Its own 2.0% growth projection for 2027 already looks too high against third-quarter tracking of 1.3% and a fourth-quarter projection of 0.8%. The likely change in Canadian guidance is toward a pause. The SNB's 10 December assessment comes with a new conditional inflation forecast. The September version already raised the medium-term path, partly because of the weaker franc. A December forecast at 0.9-1.0% for 2027 with peers still hiking would weaken the case for zero. Bloomberg Economics pencils in a possible first SNB hike in March 2027 in a high-oil scenario. Order matters: the Bank of Canada speaks on 9 December, a day before the SNB, so a soft Canadian statement followed by a firmer Swiss forecast would compound against the pair. The SNB's credibility record is strong, and with the rate at zero and inflation rising its surprise risk now leans hawkish. The SNB could restore its intervention language, which would reverse this factor.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The four-week event set has offsetting tails specific to each leg. On the Canadian side, steel and auto tariff talks were reported on 26-27 October. We put a targeted deal before year-end at 30% and a fresh escalation within four weeks at 15%, though Bank of America expects no US-Canada deal before the midterms. On the Swiss side, French political and fiscal instability keeps the OAT-Bund spread above 150bp. We put a French government collapse at about 15% over four weeks, which would be franc-positive. The Middle East is largely hedged within the cross: escalation lifts oil for CAD and haven demand for CHF, and a settlement removes both. That makes this pair less exposed to the Iran conflict than either leg is against the US dollar. Events cluster tightly in early November. The US midterms on 3 November fall on the same day as Swiss CPI, followed by the Canadian budget on 5 November and Canadian employment on 6 November. The cluster raises event volatility without a clear direction, and Swiss domestic politics, including the 29 November federal votes, carry no macro risk.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: There is a real fiscal gap but it is not currently material for this pair. Switzerland is rated AAA or Aaa stable by all three major agencies, with general government gross debt near 38% of GDP and a constitutional debt brake. Canada is rated AAA by S&P and DBRS and AA+ stable by Fitch, which projects general government debt at 92.1% of GDP in 2026. The federal budget on 5 November is the only acute fiscal event in the window. The deficit path of about C$65bn for 2026-27 is already known, and the Parliamentary Budget Officer warns it is running about C$3bn a year deeper. Only a deficit above C$75bn or a broken fiscal anchor would make this factor move CAD. The French stress that makes Swiss sovereign quality relevant against the euro does not carry over to Canada. Swiss Confederation bonds are absorbing haven demand, with the ten-year falling 11bp in October, but that matters mainly for EUR/CHF. The factor is Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months Canada's fiscal position drifts weaker while Switzerland's stays strong, but neither crosses a threshold that would move the currency. The Parliamentary Budget Officer projects Ottawa missing its declining deficit-to-GDP anchor. Federal debt charges are set to rise from C$55.6bn to C$76.1bn over five years, and higher yields will push them above that path. Fitch's AA+ already reflects debt roughly double the AA median. We put an S&P or DBRS downgrade within six months below 10%. Switzerland faces modest structural federal deficits of CHF 2-4bn a year in 2027-2029, below 0.5% of GDP, and has ample fiscal space. The gap therefore supports the franc structurally, but carry and growth price this cross, not sovereign spreads. Canadian bonds also attracted C$80.8bn of foreign buying in the second quarter, which shows no strain on demand. Neutral at slightly lower confidence reflects a background negative for Canadian bonds rather than for CAD/CHF.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The direction call was formed without the pair's chart, so the trend regime, moving averages and support and resistance zones are covered in the trade plan below rather than here. What we can assess is the options landscape. CAD/CHF has no listed option. Its implied vol is estimated from CME-listed Canadian dollar and Swiss franc options through the cross-variance identity: 4.882% at 35.7 days, 5.093% at 98.7 days and 5.339% at 189.6 days, observed 29 October. Low implied vol relative to a 250bp carry keeps the pair attractive as a carry trade in calm markets, and the skew shows hedgers paying for a franc-strength shock. Neither gives a directional signal that the rest of this analysis lacks.

Liquidity is thinner than in either USD leg: CAD/CHF trades mostly through the two dollar pairs, which widens execution costs and gap risk around events. tactical.bilateral_analysis: Dollar funding is calm and orderly, which keeps carry trades running, including franc-funded positions such as long CAD/CHF. SOFR printed 3.94% on 28-29 October inside the 3.75-4.00% target range. Reserve balances averaged about USD 2.96tn in the week to 21 October, and central bank swap-line usage is negligible at USD 170m. The Canadian dollar is insulated from basis stress: the CME Canadian dollar futures roll implies a CAD-USD basis close to zero, and Canadian banks are closely tied into US funding markets. Swiss institutions borrow dollars structurally to fund foreign assets. In a dollar squeeze the franc would weaken at first and then strengthen as carry unwinds, so the cross would face two-sided pressure. Year-end funding seasonality usually lifts dollar demand from late November, a mild risk to carry positions, but nothing points to stress before then. With no squeeze visible and the effect on this cross indirect, the factor is Neutral.

tactical.score_interpretation: A net score of -0.1291 is Bearish, but only 0.029 beyond the -0.10 threshold. It rests on depth in two factors rather than breadth. Growth and inflation (-0.1044) and risk appetite (-0.0663) outweigh the oil-driven external balance (+0.0416), and seven factors, including the 0.24-weighted policy factor, score zero. A single strong Canadian employment report on 6 November would be enough to pull the score back into Neutral.
tactical.rationale: At tactical weights the result rests on growth and inflation (0.18) and risk appetite (0.13), because the largest weight, Policy and Rates, is Neutral: neither the Bank of Canada nor the SNB meets inside four weeks. The weighted score of -0.1291 is a narrow Bearish. Canada's stalling economy, with August GDP flat, September estimated at -0.1% and 68,300 jobs lost, contrasts with Swiss growth of 2.63% on the year and Swiss inflation rising to 1.0%. That gap does most of the work, helped by wider credit spreads and a revived franc haven bid around French fiscal stress. The two currency views interact more than the near-neutral readings of each against the US dollar suggest. The Canadian dollar's tactical support comes mostly from oil and a hawkish Bank of Canada. The franc's comes from haven demand and a softer SNB intervention stance. In the cross, oil and Middle East haven demand partly cancel, which leaves the Canadian growth shortfall more exposed. Two bilateral factors moderate the call. Positive carry of 250bp, about 283bp in the futures roll, makes the pair costly to short. Leveraged funds are already heavily short the Canadian dollar, so a positive surprise would squeeze the pair higher. What is priced is a Canadian labour market stable enough for a January hike and a Swiss inflation peak near 1%. Our edge is that Canadian data on 6, 16 and 30 November are more likely to trim the first than Swiss CPI on 3 November is to disturb the second. The path of least resistance is a mild drift lower for the pair through November, slowed by carry. The key dates are Swiss CPI and the US midterms on 3 November, Canadian trade on 4 November, the budget on 5 November, employment on 6 November, CPI on 16 November, third-quarter GDP on 30 November and November employment on 4 December. Conviction is 2 rather than 3 because the score clears the threshold by under 0.03, depends on two factors, runs with an already crowded Canadian short, and must overcome positive carry. It is not 1 because the growth gap is measurable and widening.
tactical.g10_relative_ranking: As a short-CAD expression this cross ranks below CAD/NOK and AUD/CAD, where carry also favours the short. A short CAD/CHF pays about 2.8% a year, the most expensive CAD short in the G10 on carry, so it only makes sense as a growth-versus-haven trade. As a long-franc expression it ranks behind EUR/CHF, which isolates the French-stress haven bid, and roughly level with USD/CHF. Our Canadian research ranks CAD 6th of 11 tactically and our Swiss research ranks CHF 6th, so the cross is mid-table in the opportunity set and its appeal depends on the Canadian data calendar.

A targeted steel and auto tariff deal squeezes the leveraged CAD short.
Swiss CPI prints 0.8% or lower, keeping franc funding attractive.
Canadian employment falls by more than 40,000 for a third month.
The OAT-Bund spread rises above 170bp or the VIX closes above 25, forcing franc shorts to cover.

tactical.path_expectation: 3-6 November: Swiss CPI, the US midterms, Canadian trade, the budget and employment all land in four sessions. Expect a choppy start, with one 50-70 pip day around the 6 November employment report, about twice the 31-pip ATR. After a weak employment print: the pair should break the three-touch band at 0.58684-0.58867, 25 pips below spot, and drift toward 0.5850 into the 16 November CPI. Rallies before then should stall below the 29 October intraday high of 0.59295, the only meaningful overhead reference before 0.6000. Late November: a pullback toward 0.5880-0.5900 is likely as carry reasserts itself in a quiet week. Third-quarter GDP on 30 November and November employment on 4 December decide whether the month closes near 0.5850. Realised volatility should stay near 5-5.5%. The shape is a slow, carry-resisted grind lower, not a trend break.

increase_conditions: Increase to 3 if: October employment is -30,000 or weaker with unemployment at 6.6% or higher, and January Bank of Canada hike pricing falls below 50%; the Canada-Switzerland two-year spread narrows below 295bp from 313bp; and the OAT-Bund spread closes above 170bp in the same fortnight.
Increase to 4 if: two of the three conditions for 3 are met, and October CPI-trim/median averages 1.9% or less on 16 November.
decrease_conditions: Decrease to 1 if: October employment rises by more than 20,000 and unemployment is 6.4% or lower.
Decrease to 1 if: a targeted US-Canada tariff deal is announced, or Swiss CPI prints 0.7% or lower. Any of these would put the score back inside the Neutral band.

risk_reward.asymmetry_assessment: The payoff is positive but thin. Carry takes almost half the spot expected value, and the adverse case is the crowded-CAD-short squeeze. The trade is worth taking only at small size and from a better entry than spot. Trade plan: entry one-third at spot 0.5902 and two-thirds on a rally into 0.5915-0.5925 (average about 0.5913); stop on a daily close above 0.5970 (about 57 pips, 1.8 ATR, above average entry and beyond the 52-week high); targets 0.5875, 0.5850 (base case) and 0.5810 (stretch); risk 0.30% of capital on a stop distance of about 1.0% (notional about 30% of capital); halve size into the 6 November release because of gap risk in an indirect cross.

strategic.score_interpretation: A net score of -0.2682 is clearly Bearish. Four factors point the same way: the policy-gap path (-0.1248), guidance (-0.0624), growth and inflation (-0.055) and event risk (-0.026). None is offset, because the external balance, at the largest strategic weight after rates, is Neutral. Every directional factor sits at 52-55 confidence, though, so the score reflects agreement among low-confidence views more than any single strong conviction. Positive carry, which the score treats as already priced, is the main cost of acting on it.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights, Policy and Rates (0.24), External Balance (0.18) and Guidance (0.12) carry over half the weight. The outcome turns on the first and third pointing the same way while the second is balanced. The score of -0.2682 is Bearish. The core argument is that the CAD-CHF policy gap is priced to widen further while both central banks are likely to narrow it. The Canadian two-year sits 81bp above a 2.50% policy rate, yet core inflation is 1.8-1.9% and growth is tracking well below the Bank's projection, so we expect at most one more hike. The Swiss two-year at 0.18% prices almost nothing, yet headline inflation is rising from 1.0% and we put 30% on an SNB hike by March 2027. The two currency views reinforce each other in this cross. Our Canadian research is Bearish CAD and ranks it 8th of 11. Our Swiss research is mildly Bullish CHF and ranks it 4th. A pair combining a bottom-four and a top-four currency should lean toward the stronger one. Two bilateral features modify that. Oil and haven demand partly cancel in this cross, which neutralises the external balance. Positive carry of about 2.8% a year in the futures roll means forwards already discount a sizeable decline, so the bearish edge must come from repricing the policy gap rather than from the direction alone. What is priced is a widening gap, a permanent but stable Canadian tariff discount and a dormant SNB. We expect the gap to stop widening, a 25% chance of US tariff escalation on 1 January 2027, and a firmer SNB forecast. The path of least resistance is a gradual decline that accelerates around the 9 December Bank of Canada decision and the 10 December SNB assessment with its new conditional forecast. The 1 January 2027 tariff date is the main tail. The first Bank of Canada decision of 2027 is not in the published schedule we hold. Conviction is 2 because every directional factor sits at 52-55 confidence, carry works against the position, and a tariff deal would squeeze a crowded Canadian short. It is not lower because four independent factors agree.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically, CAD/CHF is one of the more coherent CAD shorts because it pairs our 8th-ranked G10 currency (CAD) with our 4th-ranked (CHF). On a carry-adjusted basis it still ranks behind CAD/NOK and AUD/CAD, where the short also earns carry. Among franc longs it ranks ahead of GBP/CHF and AUD/CHF on fundamentals but behind CHF/JPY shorts and EUR/CHF shorts. CAD/CHF is the cleanest way to express a Canadian growth and tariff shortfall against Swiss policy normalisation, at a carry cost.

conditions: The Bank of Canada holds on 9 December with softer guidance and hikes at most once more by March 2027.
The SNB's 10 December forecast puts 2027 inflation at 0.9-1.0% or higher.
Canadian growth averages below 1.5% annualised in the third and fourth quarters, with unemployment at 6.7-6.8%.
The 1 January 2027 tariff decision is no better than the status quo.
base_case.path: A fall of 152 pips (-2.58%) from 0.59021 into the 0.57167-0.57617 band that contains the 200-day. Phase 1, November to 8 December: a 0.5840-0.5930 range as Canadian data trim hike pricing against carry support. Phase 2, 9-10 December: a soft Bank of Canada statement followed by a firmer SNB forecast takes the pair into the 0.57811-0.58232 band, around 0.5800-0.5820. Phase 3, the 1 January 2027 tariff date: the largest tail, with thin late-December liquidity raising gap risk either way. Phase 4, January to April 2027: the first Bank of Canada decision of the year (date not yet published) and fourth-quarter GDP on 1 March carry the pair to 0.5750, with pullbacks to 0.5870-0.5890 likely after carry-driven rebounds.

The US raises tariffs on Canadian steel and cars to 50% on 1 January 2027.
The SNB signals or delivers a March 2027 hike.
A euro-area sovereign or credit shock forces franc-funded carry to unwind.

Pullbacks to 0.5870-0.5890 are likely after carry-driven rebounds. The shape is a stepped decline around event dates, separated by carry-driven drift higher. It is not a smooth trend.

The trade pays only if the December repricing or the tariff tail arrives early enough to shorten the holding period. Defined-risk structures that pay in the 25% downside tail are the more efficient expression. consensus_divergence.our_tactical_view: Bearish CAD/CHF over four weeks (score -0.1291, conviction 2), driven by Canada's growth shortfall against Swiss inflation and growth, and by a revived franc haven bid.
consensus_divergence.our_strategic_view: Bearish CAD/CHF over one to six months (score -0.2682, conviction 2), on a CAD-CHF policy gap priced to widen that we expect to stop widening, softer Bank of Canada guidance against a firmer SNB forecast, and the 1 January 2027 US tariff tail.
consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: Not measurable against a pair consensus, because no bank research publishes a CAD/CHF forecast that we could locate. Our view matches leg-level bank caution on CAD and goes against leg-level forecasts for a weaker franc.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Not quantifiable. Crossing one bank's USD/CAD forecast with another's USD/CHF forecast would manufacture a consensus that does not exist, so we do not state a figure.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: At the leg level, National Bank of Canada is cautious on the Canadian dollar through year-end, citing a WCS discount that limits Canada's oil gain and the risks from trade tensions. Commerzbank and Bank of America are both sceptical that the Bank of Canada can deliver the tightening markets price. We agree with them, and weight that scepticism through the policy-gap path rather than the level of the differential. On the franc we differ from bank forecasts for a weaker franc into year-end, such as UBS's EUR/CHF recovery call cited in our Swiss research. Those forecasts predate the SNB dropping its increased willingness to intervene and the rise in Swiss inflation to 1.0%, both of which we weight more heavily. Non-bank context (retail aggregators, not bank research): one survey page aggregating two providers, updated 15 October, has CHF/CAD at 1.7247 year-end 2026 then 1.7125 mid-2027, implying CAD/CHF of about 0.5798 and 0.5839, directionally the same as this analysis; a broker's weekly note on 1 November puts the expected range for the week ahead at 0.5810 to 0.5976, which brackets our tactical scenarios.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: If both banks narrow the expected policy gap and the tariff tail materialises, the pair falls by more than the roughly 2.8% annualised carry deducted in forwards. The policy-gap repricing pays at the December decisions and the tariff tail pays in early January.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If the Bank of Canada delivers two more hikes as oil holds above USD 100, or a US-Canada tariff deal lands, a crowded Canadian short squeezes and the pair rises while the short also pays about 2.8% a year in carry.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: Both horizons are Bearish, but for different reasons. Tactically the call rests on Canadian data against Swiss inflation and a haven bid, and it barely clears the threshold. Strategically it rests on the policy-gap path, guidance and the tariff calendar, and four factors agree. The strategic view is more robust because it does not depend on a single employment report.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: None required; both horizons point the same way. The 9-10 December Bank of Canada and SNB sequence is where the strategic case is most likely to be confirmed or rejected.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: The tactical call is fragile and the strategic call is sturdier but costs carry. The bearish view is best built gradually into the 9-10 December central bank sequence rather than all at once before the 6 November employment report. The tactical position is sized at 0.30% of capital at risk, scaled in on rallies toward 0.5915-0.5925 and halved into 6 November; the strategic position adds its final third only after the 10 December SNB forecast. Where the price data pushes back: the pair has rallied 3.31% in six months while Canadian fundamentals deteriorated and sits at the 94th percentile of its closing range above a bullishly stacked daily average set. The driver is the carry flow that market commentary describes as the franc's new funding-currency role, and the SNB itself said the fall was in line with widened interest rate differentials, with little safe-haven demand since June. That flow is scored as balanced positioning, not as direction, which is correct as a matter of method, but it means the tactical call needs a catalyst: a weak 6 November print or a French stress spike. A calm November is likely to favour carry over the score. The strategic call, resting on four agreeing factors and dated December catalysts, is better founded than the tactical one, which should be read as a timing call on the Canadian data calendar, not a forecast that the carry bid fades by itself.

forward_vs_spot.edge_3m: -60 pips (our expected rate below the forward; bearish edge). At one month the edge is -38 pips against an expected 0.5850, just over one ATR and too small to act on alone.
forward_vs_spot.edge_6m: -69 pips (our expected rate below the forward; a real but modest edge that depends on the December policy repricing). On the pure 250bp policy gap the six-month forward would be 0.58283, making the edge about 78 pips.

catalysts.rationale: September headline was 1.0% and core 0.5%. A print of 1.2% or higher would revive December SNB hike pricing from about 6bp and lower CAD/CHF. A print of 0.8% or lower would confirm the SNB hold and support the pair through carry. We expect 1.0-1.1%, close to pricing.

The result shapes the room for a US-Canada tariff deal and the Fed path. A dovish dollar repricing would support carry and risk-sensitive currencies over havens, lifting the pair. A risk-off reaction in US equities would favour the franc.

This is the first full month of WTI above USD 90, which should keep the Canadian surplus above C$3bn after August's C$4.2bn. A large surplus confirms the oil-driven terms-of-trade gain, the main near-term support for the Canadian leg against an energy-importing Switzerland.

The deficit path of about C$65bn for 2026-27 is known, and the Parliamentary Budget Officer warns it is running about C$3bn a year deeper. Only a deficit above C$75bn or a broken fiscal anchor would weigh on CAD against the AAA-rated franc.

We expect a third straight employment decline and unemployment at 6.6%, against a market pricing a January Bank of Canada hike on stabilisation. A gain would instead squeeze the crowded leveraged CAD short and lift the pair, making this the highest-stakes tactical release for the cross.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada summary of deliberations on the 28 October decision (week of 9 November)
catalysts.rationale: The summary will show whether a December pause was discussed or most members wanted to signal further hikes. A pause discussion would start removing the priced widening in the CAD-CHF gap ahead of the 9 December decision, while hawkish language would support the carry bid.

We expect headline near 3.2% on gasoline and CPI-trim and CPI-median at 1.8-2.0%. Core below 2% weakens the case for a second hike and narrows the expected CAD-CHF policy gap, which weighs on the pair.

catalysts.event: Swiss Q3 GDP (SECO flash), week of 23 November (exact date not stated)
catalysts.rationale: The second quarter's 1.5% gain was driven by pharmaceuticals, and a sharp third-quarter slowdown is expected. A flat or negative print would narrow the growth gap that drives the tactical score and lower the odds of a 2027 SNB hike, supporting the pair. A firm print would reinforce the growth divergence.

catalysts.event: Canadian GDP, third quarter and September
catalysts.rationale: Industry data put third-quarter growth near 1.3% annualised against the Bank of Canada's 2.0%. A print below 1.5% confirms the growth shortfall that drives our bearish view of the growth gap with Switzerland.

This is the last employment report before the 9 December Bank of Canada decision. A fourth decline would cement the hold and push any second hike out of early 2027. A rebound would revive it and support the pair.

A hold is priced. The risk is in the statement: guidance softer than October's 'could be a need' language would remove part of the priced widening in the CAD-CHF gap. This is a bare decision without a Monetary Policy Report, and it comes one day before the SNB.

catalysts.event: SNB quarterly monetary policy assessment with new conditional inflation forecast
catalysts.rationale: This is the higher-stakes of the two December dates for this pair. A conditional forecast showing 2027 inflation at 0.9-1.0% or higher, or any hint of a 2027 hike, would narrow the expected policy gap and lower CAD/CHF. A return to intervention language would do the opposite.

catalysts.event: Threatened increase of US tariffs on Canadian steel and cars to 50%
catalysts.rationale: We put escalation at 25% and a targeted deal beforehand at 35%. Escalation would hit Canadian growth and widen the tariff discount on CAD with no Swiss equivalent. A deal would squeeze the crowded Canadian short and lift the pair sharply.

invalidators.mechanism: The event tail behind Factor 7 would disappear, and the most stretched short in the cross (CAD leveraged -96,747 contracts) would cover into a pair with positive carry and no real-money seller.

invalidators.mechanism: It would mean the market is pricing the policy gap wider still on Canadian hikes, against our thesis that both banks narrow it. That would remove the largest strategic contribution (Factor 1, -0.1248).

invalidators.condition: The average of CPI-trim and CPI-median rises above 2.3% in the November or December Canadian CPI.
invalidators.mechanism: Core inflation above target would validate a two-hike Bank of Canada path to 3.00% and widen the CAD-CHF gap rather than narrow it, reversing Factors 1, 2 and 6 together.

invalidators.mechanism: Falling Swiss inflation removes the SNB's 2027 hike option, keeps the franc anchored as the G10's preferred funding currency, and leaves only the Canadian leg carrying the bearish case.

invalidators.condition: The SNB restores its increased willingness to intervene, or domestic sight deposits rise more than CHF 10bn in four weeks (above CHF 445bn from CHF 435.36bn).
invalidators.mechanism: Renewed franc selling would cap franc strength across every cross and reverse the strategic guidance divergence (Factor 6).
invalidators.monitor_indicator: SNB weekly sight deposits and policy statements

invalidators.condition: WTI holds above USD 115 for four weeks with the WCS discount narrower than USD 15.
invalidators.mechanism: A realised Canadian barrel near USD 100 would lift the external balance to a strategic positive on the 0.18 weight. In this cross the oil gain is not offset by matching haven demand unless escalation accompanies it.

invalidators.new_stance: Close the tactical and strategic positions (execution invalidator; the scored stance changes only if one of the fundamental conditions above is met)
invalidators.mechanism: Such a move would mean the carry bid is overpowering the fundamental case faster than the December catalysts can arrive, and it would lift the falling 200-week average into play as the next reference.

signposts.bilateral_importance: This is the cross's own rate-path gauge. Each leg's spread to Treasuries mixes in US policy; this one isolates the Bank of Canada against the SNB, the core of the strategic thesis.

signposts.current_level: December hold; 25bp to 2.75% fully priced by January (30 October 2026)
signposts.invalidates_if: A December hike priced above 60%, or a third hike priced by mid-2027
signposts.bilateral_importance: With the SNB near zero and dormant, nearly all of the priced widening in the CAD-CHF gap sits on the Canadian side. This pricing is the single input that moves the cross's forward points.

signposts.confirms_if: Headline at or above 1.1% with core at or above 0.6%
signposts.bilateral_importance: Rising Swiss inflation is the only route by which the SNB narrows the 250bp gap from its side. For this pair it matters more than for EUR/CHF, where French stress dominates.

signposts.bilateral_importance: The tactical score rests mainly on the growth gap, and Canadian employment is also the trigger for the cross's largest squeeze risk, the 96,747-contract leveraged CAD short.

signposts.invalidates_if: The CAD short falls below -50,000 contracts
signposts.bilateral_importance: The cross's crowding is the difference between the two legs. Asymmetric covering, CAD shorts holding while franc shorts close, is the positioning picture that would confirm a falling pair.

assumptions: The analysis uses daily open, high, low and close prices for CAD/CHF over 130 weekday sessions from 2026-05-04 to 2026-10-30. Spot is 0.59021 at the 30 October close. No weekend bars were in the delivered series.

The valuation date of 1 November 2026 is a Sunday, so the two days between the last close and the valuation date are a weekend and no trading session was missed. Every level, pip distance, percentage and forward outright in the report is computed against 0.59021.

Moving averages, support and resistance zones and the 200-week figures are computed over the full price history of 4,920 weekday sessions from 2007-12-24 to 2026-10-30 (1,011 weekly and 502 monthly bars). The 130 sessions shown cover the one-to-six-month strategic horizon and are used for the recent price-action narrative and for higher-high/higher-low structure.
Moving averages are simple averages of trading-day closes. Realised volatility is annualised on 252 trading days. ATR(14) is 31 pips.

Support and resistance zones are clusters of weekly and monthly swing closes, ranked by touch count. Their stated distances are measured from spot to each band's midpoint; the support and resistance levels in the structured fields are band midpoints, with the 29 October intraday high 0.59295 as the nearest overhead reference.

Performance windows are the supplied figures: 1 month +1.00%, 3 months +2.60%, 6 months +3.31%, 1 year +3.56%. The 52-week percentile quoted (94th) is on a closing basis; the intraday-basis figure is 92nd.

The daily central-bank policy series shows the Bank of Canada at 2.25% as of 26 October and the SNB at 0% as of 27 October. The Canadian figure lags the 28 October hike, so the report uses 2.50% and a 250bp differential throughout.

The ten-year yields in that series (Canada 3.8825%, Switzerland 0.59%) are monthly averages dated 1 September 2026. They are not live levels and are used only alongside end-October closes of 3.799% and 0.47%.

CAD/CHF implied volatility (4.882%, 5.093% and 5.339% at 35.7, 98.7 and 189.6 days, observed 29 October) is an estimate built from listed Canadian dollar and Swiss franc options with a realised correlation of 0.6371 standing in for implied correlation. It has historically run 9-18% low, so it is treated as a floor. The three-month figure is measured at 98.7 days, not 90. No implied-volatility percentile is stated because the cross has no quoted history. Leg risk reversals are used to infer cross skew.

Forward points use the -283.1bp annualised premium between the December 2026 and March 2027 listed futures, observed 29 October (near leg 46.7 days, far leg 137.6 days). By covered interest parity this combines the expected rate differential with any cross-currency basis, which cannot be separated without an OIS curve. It is not the policy differential.
Weight adjustments are on Factors 3 (+0.03), 5 (+0.02) and 10 (-0.05) on both horizons, for the bilateral reasons stated in the weight table. Both horizons sum to 1.00.

No factor stance rests on this pair's own recent price action. Price data is used only for market context, entries, targets, stops, sizing, invalidator levels and the unscored chart context under Factor 9.

PPP comparisons use World Bank conversion factors flagged as best available. REER percentiles cover the 33 monthly BIS readings since January 2024. CFTC percentiles cover the 25 weekly reports since May 2026.

Bilateral goods trade is the 2024 IMF Direction of Trade data supplied: Canadian exports to Switzerland USD 4.6bn and imports USD 5.8bn, a net balance of -USD 1.2bn. The gap to Swiss-reported imports from Canada (USD 8.5bn) is attributed to gold shipments as an inference.
Scenario probabilities are fixed at 50/25/25. Probabilities for central bank decisions, tariff outcomes and stress events are this analysis's own estimates unless described as market pricing.
The first Bank of Canada decision of 2027 and the SNB's March 2027 assessment are referred to without firm dates where the published schedule does not yet carry them.
